But since Morris declared on Wednesday, their assessment has gotten rosier. Morris has improved dramatically since high school and may be the most improved player in college basketball. NBA executives tend to love big point guards, and Morris is the biggest true point guard in the draft.

That was noticeable the second we walked in the gym. Morris is a legit 6-foot-5 in shoes. He has broad shoulders and has a power game that's reminiscent of a young Andre Miller. Anyone who has watched Morris play knows he can make the spectacular pass and really knows how to run a team. The question marks are around his jump shot and his lateral quickness.

While Morris doesn't possess the shooting touch of Kyrie Irving or the speed of Kemba Walker, he showed on Wednesday that he's better at both than he's given credit for (video here). While he's not an elite athlete, he's quicker with the ball than you think and shows great control with his handle. Morris also showed off a terrific midrange jumper in drills. His NBA 3-point shot was solid but still needs work.

Morris has elite size and may have the best court vision of anyone in the draft. Add in his defensive abilities and a great, supportive family background, and I can see Morris sticking in the first round. For Georgia's Travis Leslie, an undersized guard who has forward skills, this plays a big part in projecting him as a first-round talent.

May 13 Update: The draft may be weak on true centers this year, but two players -- Fresno State's Greg Smith and Oakland's Keith Benson -- did their best to try to make their claim that they should be first-rounders.

The two couldn't be more different. Smith is a physical specimen. He's a 6-foot-10, 250-pound power player with a 7-foot-3 wingspan and just 6.4 percent body fat. He had the biggest hands (11.25 inches) of anyone at the New Jersey workouts and recorded a 35.5-inch vertical -- a terrific number for a player his size. However, he is still pretty raw offensively.

Benson is taller and a more fluid athlete. He runs the floor well and is pretty quick laterally for a big man. He lacks the strength and explosiveness of Smith, but makes up for it with a pretty polished perimeter game for a player his size.

Motor could be an issue for both players. In college, neither played hard all the time. Smith got lost at times on the offensive end, and Benson gained a bad rep from scouts for his defensive play.

But the upside is there for both players, depending on what you're looking for. Smith is going to be a project, but his physical tools may make him worth it -- Daniel Orton went as a first-rounder with a similar tool set. Benson needs to get stronger and show a willingness to be physical, but he has unique skills for a guy his size.

Right now, neither player is listed in our mock draft as a first-rounder, but bigs tend to rise as we get closer to the draft, and both may get a look late in the first round.

Jan 20 Update: The other potential sleeper I've been locking in on lately is considerably more well-known than Xavier Silas for a few reasons. Holiday plays for the Washington Huskies in the Pac-10, and his brother, Jrue Holiday, is one of the best young players in the NBA (currently playing for the Philadelphia 76ers). Like a few players each season, Justin Holiday has thrust himself into draft consideration as a senior after an average three-year career. he's showing that he has the tools to be a long-time pro. Justin Holiday has always been a stopper, but his improved 3-point shot will have scouts intrigued. What Holiday brings to the table is a rare combination: size and length for his position, solid athleticism, excellent 3-point shooting, good skills as a passer and lockdown abilities as a defender. I'm not sure there is another strong defensive prospect in the draft that has made better than 44 percent of his treys. That fact alone could make him a second-round pick.

Holiday's improvement as a shooter is impressive. Check the evolution for Holiday's 3-point shooting over the first three years of his career: 0-for-5, 1-for-4, 10-for-30. He is 29-for-65 so far this season, and with this kind of progress it's easy to project significant improvement over the next three to five years -- not in terms of his shooting percentages, but rather his overall game. Only genuine hard work delivers improvement that significant, so as he targets new weaknesses we can expect he'll have at least some degree of success.

Holiday is not quite a point forward, but he's close. He makes easy passes to help keep the Huskies' offense moving, and he can throw a laser for an assist, as well. In the NBA, he can play next to primary scorers at both guard spots and not detract from their numbers because he's used to only taking good shots that are set up for him. Being a primary scorer is not his mindset. Because of his shooting and passing skills, he can definitely play some shooting guard in the league. I like him best as a slightly undersized small forward, with his length mitigating any issues stemming from his having a short neck (hence a smaller than 6-foot-7 measurement).

Holiday has a chance to be an excellent defender -- one that's capable of defending all three perimeter positions. His length, hoops IQ, feel and attitude contribute to his success. He's a guy who will almost always make the right reads when executing the defensive game plan, and he is someone who will relish being a "stopper."

At this point, I'd be surprised to see Holiday go below 45 or so in the draft. He could inch higher, but the 40-50 range seems like a pretty solid floor for him. Getting a guy like Holiday in the second round is gold to NBA GMs, who are always looking to add "drafting a sleeper" to their resumes. -- By David Thorpe
